clue.text: Have fun exciting two lasses in wood?

indicators.note: exciting means stirring up, so the letters of the following words are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A man enjoying himself by thrilling two young women in a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exciting' is the anagram signal working on all fifteen letters of TWO LASSES IN WOOD; the picture of fun in the woods suits the phrase nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a young person indulging in wild, carefree behaviour before settling down, i.e. having fun.

clue.text: Given little money, appear grateful having secured British home for the National Theatre

parts.note: a sou is an old French coin of small value, hence a little money

indicators.note: having secured means holding something fast, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to thank someone is to show that you are grateful

explanation.surface: Someone tipped a small sum shows gratitude for a British venue housing the National Theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The South Bank is the arts district on the south side of the Thames in London where the National Theatre stands.
explanation.definitionFit: The National Theatre's building stands on London's South Bank, so the district is literally its home.

clue.text: One's charged a bundle of money to trap bird

indicators.note: to trap means to hold captive, so the bird sits caught inside the bundle

parts.note: a wad is a roll or bundle of banknotes
the rhea is a large flightless South American bird

explanation.surface: Someone is billed a large sum of money for catching a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' suggests a price, but the definition means carrying an explosive charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A warhead is the explosive part of a missile, the thing that carries the charge.

clue.text: Curiosity has no function on ship

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the ship comes last

parts.note: sine is a trigonometric function
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Inquisitiveness serves no purpose aboard a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosiness is prying interest in other people's affairs, a nagging form of inquisitiveness.

clue.text: Ultimate in father figures, upstanding European chap

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards
the ultimate letter in a word is its final one

parts.note: ones are figures, single digits

explanation.surface: The best of the father figures is a decent, upright European man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upstanding' looks like praise for the man but turns R plus ONES round to give the Spanish title.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is the Spanish word for a gentleman or Mr, so a man from Spain, a European.

clue.text: That's small and thick? Grow up!

definitions.meaning: taken literally, the phrase says the thing is neither large nor bright
the stock rebuke to someone behaving childishly

annotation.spelling: IT'S NOT BIG AND IT'S NOT CLEVER

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a thing as tiny and stupid, then tells the person to act their age.
explanation.walkthrough: The well-worn British put-down is read first word by word (not big = small, not clever = thick) and then as the reprimand it really is.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase scolds silly behaviour, so it works as a telling-off urging maturity; literally it describes something little and dim.

clue.text: Fool reciting 11 and 25 after this in book?

definitions.text: reciting 11 and 25 after this in book?
definitions.meaning: saying this word followed by the answers to 11 and 25 (a garden tool and a Scottish river) sounds like the title of Cervantes' novel about the deluded knight

explanation.surface: An idiot reads out two other answers in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is HOE and 25 is TAY; spoken after this word they give 'Donkey Hoe-tay', a jokey pronunciation of Don Quixote.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a donkey means they are foolish, a dim ass.

clue.text: Bitter hiding place for missionary

indicators.note: hiding means concealing, so the beer wraps around the place

parts.note: bitter is a type of ale, a British beer
a post is a position or place, as in a job

explanation.surface: A pint of bitter conceals a hiding spot for a preacher.
explanation.walkthrough: BITTER is a hoppy British beer, a kind of ale.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostles were the first Christian missionaries, and the word is used of anyone spreading a faith.

clue.text: Very fine, but not entirely speedy

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'

indicators.note: not entirely means one letter short of complete, so the final letter goes

parts.note: nice means fine or pleasant

explanation.surface: Something is excellent, though not wholly quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonic relates to sound, and by extension speeds near the speed of sound, hence speedy, as in Sonic the Hedgehog.

clue.text: Lever in middle of lounge, lifted

indicators.note: in says the lever goes inside the central letters
the middle of a six-letter word is its central pair of letters

parts.note: to prise is to lever something open

explanation.surface: A lever sitting in the centre of a sitting room has been raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Uprisen is an old-fashioned past participle meaning having risen up, so raised or lifted.

clue.text: Loose woman's first to break up partners at the end of the day

indicators.note: to break up a pair is to come between them, so the other letters split the partners

parts.note: South and North are partners at the bridge table, abbreviated S and N
to undo is to loosen or unfasten

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A promiscuous woman comes between a couple by evening.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are North, South, East and West, and North and South play as partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundown is the time the sun sets, which marks the close of daylight.

clue.text: Tool knocking head off pump, perhaps

indicators.note: knocking the head off a word removes its first letter

parts.note: a pump is a light shoe, an example of footwear

explanation.surface: An implement strikes the top off a water pump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pump' suggests a water pump, but here it is the light shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoe is a long-handled garden implement for weeding.

clue.text: One's likely to drop off Eric Clapton after taking a spin

indicators.note: a spin whirls things round, so the guitarist's name is spun into a new order

explanation.surface: The guitarist tends to nod off after a drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A narcoleptic person suffers sudden attacks of sleep, so is prone to dozing without warning.

clue.text: Reckon one's reaching a sweet African city

parts.note: to add is to reckon up a sum
one is I, and the 's stands for is
a baba is a rum-soaked sponge cake, a sweet

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they are heading for a sweet treat.
explanation.definitionFit: Addis Ababa is the capital of Ethiopia, a city in the Horn of Africa.

clue.text: Crew member heading for bathroom, then waits on a potty

indicators.note: the heading for a word is its first letter
potty means crazy, so the following letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A sailor heads to the loo, then attends to a chamber pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' looks like a child's toilet, fitting the bathroom, but it is the British word for crazy, signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A boatswain is the ship's officer in charge of rigging and deck crew, a member of the crew.

clue.text: Connect Maltese and Spanish borders

indicators.note: borders are the edges, so the first and last letters of each word are taken

explanation.surface: Join up the frontiers of Malta and Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Gears mesh when their teeth interlock, so the verb means fit together or link.

clue.text: Try to hold on with extra climbing, as arboreal mammal

indicators.note: to hold means to contain, so the court word wraps around the rest

parts.note: to hear a case is to try it in court
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means rising from the bottom, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a bye is an extra in cricket, a run scored without the ball being hit

explanation.surface: Attempting to hang on with something extra while going up, like a tree-dwelling animal.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bye is a run taken when the ball passes the batsman without being hit, counted among the extras.
explanation.definitionFit: The honey bear, another name for the kinkajou or sun bear, lives in trees, so it is a tree-dwelling animal.

clue.text: Whole jumbo jet then ends up south of island

indicators.note: in a down clue, south of means placed below, so the island comes first
in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: jumbo means large

indicators.note: the ends of two words are their final letters

explanation.surface: A jumbo jet as a whole ends up to the south of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends' takes the last letters of 'jet' and 'then', T and N, and 'up' turns LARGETN round to NTEGRAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral means essential to completeness, so forming a whole or complete unit.

clue.text: Some bike pinched, in gendarme's possession

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of a stolen bicycle is now held by a French policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: A kepi is the flat-topped peaked cap worn by French police and soldiers, so an item a gendarme owns.

clue.text: Bird requires school to catch fish

indicators.note: to catch means to enclose, so the school wraps around the fish

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
char is a fish related to the trout

explanation.surface: A bird needs a school of fish to hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: The pochard is a diving duck, a species of waterbird.

clue.text: Badger bait sent back, large cask having snared a mammoth

indicators.note: sent back means returned, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: to badger is to nag
to rag is to tease or bait someone

indicators.note: having snared means having caught, so the cask encloses the letter

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: Bait for badgers is returned, with a big barrel having caught a woolly mammoth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gargantuan and mammoth are both adjectives meaning enormous, after Rabelais's giant.

clue.text: Old raconteur seen one month after the second half of another?

indicators.note: after says the trimmed month comes before the rest
keeping the second half means dropping the first three letters

parts.note: another month here is August
I is the Roman numeral for one
Nov is the abbreviation for November

explanation.surface: An old storyteller appears one month after the latter part of another month.
explanation.walkthrough: The other month is AUGUST, whose second half is UST; Peter Ustinov was a British actor celebrated for his anecdotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Peter Ustinov, who died in 2004, was famous as a witty teller of stories on chat shows.

clue.text: Bacon, say, last of meat eaten by short lady, perhaps?

indicators.note: eaten by means swallowed, so the letter goes inside the shortened noble
short means cut off at the end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a lady is an example of an aristo, an aristocrat

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A small woman eats the end of some bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon' looks like meat, fitting the surface, but it is the painter Francis Bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon was a twentieth-century Irish-born British painter, an example of a painter.

clue.text: Erotic love's surprisingly sedentary

indicators.note: surprisingly means in an unexpected way, so the letters land in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken with its S

explanation.surface: Erotic love turns out, unexpectedly, to involve little movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Locorestive is a rare word for staying in one place, not inclined to move, much like sedentary.

clue.text: It's beastly in the morning, everyone getting up

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means rising from the bottom, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for morning hours
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Something is horrible early in the day when everyone has to rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' seems to mean nasty but means being a beast, an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A llama is a South American pack animal, i.e. a beast, so it is something that is beastly.

clue.text: Batting position entered

parts.note: in cricket the side batting is said to be in
to set something is to position it

explanation.surface: A cricketer's place in the batting order has been recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the team or player currently batting is described as 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inset as a verb means set into something, inserted, so a thing inset has been put in.

clue.text: Wait to drop two rivers — for one?

indicators.note: to drop means to let fall, so these letters are taken out

parts.note: to tarry is to linger or wait
R is the abbreviation for river, so two rivers give two Rs

explanation.surface: Someone lingers before dropping two rivers, as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back to 'rivers': the Tay is one, Scotland's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tay, flowing through Perth and Dundee, is itself an instance of the rivers just mentioned.

clue.text: A writer in a newspaper cut the coffee

indicators.note: in says the pen goes inside the shortened paper
cut means trimmed, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: a rag is a slang name for a low-quality newspaper
a Bic is a ballpoint pen, something that writes

explanation.surface: A columnist for a paper has cut the coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' and 'the coffee' both suggest the surface means coffee prepared or diluted, but 'cut' only trims the tabloid word, and 'the coffee' names the bean.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabica is the main species of coffee plant, and the beans sold under that name.

clue.text: Funny second series on television's beginning

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another follows it
the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a range is a series or line of products

explanation.surface: A second comedy series starts on television.
explanation.definitionFit: Funny in the sense of odd or peculiar, as in 'a funny feeling', means strange.

clue.text: See 5
